# AI/ML Engineer — Skills and Requirements

## Role Overview
An AI/ML Engineer designs, builds, and deploys machine learning models and AI systems. They work at the intersection of software engineering and data science.

## Core Technical Skills

### Programming Languages
- Python (primary language for ML/AI development)
- SQL (data querying and analysis)
- R (statistical analysis, optional)

### Machine Learning Libraries
- Scikit-learn: classification, regression, clustering, pipelines
- XGBoo

Machine Learning Libraries
- Scikit-learn: classification, regression, clustering, pipelines
- XGBoost / LightGBM: gradient boosting for tabular data
- Pandas, NumPy: data manipulation and numerical computing
- Matplotlib, Seaborn: data visualization

### Deep Learning Frameworks
- PyTorch: preferred for research and custom architectures
- TensorFlow / Keras: production deployment and mobile
- Hugging Face Transformers: pre-trained NLP models

# Career Paths in Technology — AI/ML, Backend, and Full Stack

## AI/ML Career Paths

### Path 1: ML Engineer
Focus: Building and deploying ML models in production
Skills: Python, scikit-learn, PyTorch, FastAPI, Docker, AWS
Progression: Junior ML Engineer → ML Engineer → Senior ML Engineer → Staff ML Engineer

### Path 2: Data Scientist
Focus: Insights from data, statistical modeling, business decisions
Skills: Python/R, statistics, visualization, SQL, Jupyter, Tableau

### Path 3: AI Research Scientist

Skills: Deep math, PyTorch, paper reading/writing, experiment design
Progression: Research Intern → Research Scientist → Senior Research Scientist

## Backend Career Path

Progression: Junior Backend Developer → Backend Developer → Senior → Tech Lead → Engineering Manager

Key skills at each level:
- Junior: REST APIs, basic SQL, one backend framework
- Mid: System design basics, microservices, caching, authentication
- Senior: Distributed systems, database optimization, architecture decisions
- Lead: Team mentorship, cross-team coordination, roadmap planning

## Full Stack Career Path

Progression: Junior Full Stack → Full Stack Developer → Senior Full Stack → Tech Lead

## How to Transition into AI/ML

### From Backend Development
1. Learn Python if not already proficient
2. Study ML fundamentals (Andrew Ng's ML course)
3. Build 2-3 ML projects using your existing backend skills
4. Learn FastAPI + ML model serving
5. Add ML/AI to your existing backend projects

### From Data Analysis
1. Learn Python (pandas, numpy, matplotlib)
2. Study machine learning algorithms
3. Start with simple models on familiar datasets
4. Learn deep learning

machine learning algorithms
3. Start with simple models on familiar datasets
4. Learn deep learning basics
5. Build projects that combine analysis + ML modeling

### From Fresh Graduate
1. Complete one strong ML course (fast.ai or Andrew Ng)
2. Build 3-5 end-to-end projects
3. Participate in Kaggle competitions
4. Contribute to open source
5. Network on LinkedIn and attend meetups

# Technical Interview Preparation Guide — AI/ML and Software Engineering

## Types of Interviews

### 1. Technical Screening (30–45 min)
- Basic coding questions (arrays, strings, loops)
- Questions about your resume and projects
- Conceptual ML/AI questions
- Usually conducted by a recruiter or junior engineer

### 2. Technical Deep Dive (60–90 min)
- Data structures and algorithms (LeetCode style)
- System design for experienced candidates (3+ years)
- ML fundamentals and model evaluation

## Core ML Topics to Prepare

### Supervised Learning
- Linear/Logistic Regression: assumptions, regularization (L1/L2)
- Decision Trees, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting
- Support Vector Machines
- When to use which algorithm

### Model Evaluation
- Train/validation/test split rationale
- Cross-validation: k-fold, stratified k-fold
- Metrics: accu

Train/validation/test split rationale
- Cross-validation: k-fold, stratified k-fold
- Metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC
- Confusion matrix interpretation
- Handling class imbalance (SMOTE, class_weight)

### Feature Engineering
- Handling missing values
- Encoding categorical variables (one-hot, target encoding)
- Feature scaling (StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler)
- Feature selection techniques

### Overfitting and Regularization
- Bias-variance tradeoff
- L1 (Lasso), L2 (Ridge), El

techniques

# Resume Improvement Guide for Software and AI/ML Engineers

## Why Resumes Get Rejected

Most resumes are rejected in under 10 seconds because:
1. Missing keywords from the job description
2. No quantified achievements (just responsibilities)
3. Poor formatting that fails ATS scanners
4. Generic objective statements instead of specific skills
5. Missing GitHub links or project demonstrations

## Resume Structure for Engineers

### Contact Section
- Full name, email, phone number
- LinkedIn URL

Resume Structure for Engineers

### Contact Section
- Full name, email, phone number
- LinkedIn URL (linkedin.com/in/yourname)
- GitHub URL (github.com/yourname)
- Portfolio or personal website (optional)
- Location (city, country — not full address)

### Professional Summary (2–3 lines)
Write a targeted summary matching the job you're applying to.
Example: "Python developer with 3 years of experience building ML pipelines and REST APIs. Proficient in scikit-learn, FastAPI, and PostgreSQL. Looki

ence building ML pipelines and REST APIs. Proficient in scikit-learn, FastAPI, and PostgreSQL. Looking for an AI/ML Engineer role."

### Skills Section
List skills in categories:
- Languages: Python, JavaScript, SQL
- ML/AI: scikit-learn, PyTorch, LangChain, FAISS
- Backend: FastAPI, Flask, REST APIs
- Databases: PostgreSQL, MongoDB
- Cloud: AWS, GCP
- Tools: Git, Docker, Jupyter

## ATS Optimization Tips

1. Match keywords from the job description exactly
2. Avoid tables, images, headers/footers (ATS cannot parse them)
3. Use standard section headings (Experience, Education, Skills)
4. Save as PDF unless the emplo

4. Save as PDF unless the employer specifies Word format
5. Use standard fonts (Arial, Calibri, Times New Roman)
6. Keep to 1-2 pages maximum

## Common Resume Mistakes

- Using "Responsible for..." instead of action verbs
- No GitHub link for a developer role
- Skills section lists technologies you barely know
- No quantified results (how many users, what improvement, what scale)
- Outdated skills (e.g., listing Python 2)
